h: Bluidy Tam, the Devil and a game of cards
p: Every old house needs a larger-than-life character, and the Binns has General Tam Dalyell, known as Bluidy Tam. A staunch Royalist, he was captured after the Battle of Worcester in 1651 and locked up in the Tower of London, but managed to escape. He then went off to serve the Tsar of Russia for years before returning to Scotland, where he became commander-in-chief and raised the regiment that became the Royal Scots Greys. His fierce treatment of the Covenanters earned him that grim nickname.

Then there's the legend. Tam is said to have played cards with the Devil, and beaten him. The furious Devil supposedly flung the heavy marble table at his head, missed, and it ended up in the pond. The story goes that when the pond dried out in a drought in the late nineteenth century, a marble table really was found in the mud. True or not, it's a cracking tale to tell the kids on the walk up.

The family has kept producing notable figures. Tam Dalyell, the long-serving Labour MP who gave his name to the West Lothian Question, a famous puzzle about devolution, lived here until his death in 2017.
The tower on the hill is a folly built in the 1820s, and like many follies, it has its own story about being built to settle a wager. Allow two to three hours for the tour and a walk up to it.
Blackness Castle is just a few minutes down the road, making an easy pairing, and Hopetoun House and the historic town of Bo'ness are also close by for a full day out in West Lothian.
